That's it, baker. Melchizedek is the one giving the blessing. The writer says he met Abraham, forefather of Israel, coming back from the slaughter of the kings, "and blessed him" (Hebrews 7:1). Hold onto who blesses whom, because the writer builds on it a few verses later.

Yes, baker! The writer says Melchizedek is "like the Son of God" and "remains a priest for all time" (Hebrews 7:3). Notice he says LIKE. He's pointing at a resemblance, so I'm keeping my words right there with his. I'm just here to stamp cookies, friend, and even I can see that's a big comparison.

I see why Aaron comes to mind, since we're talking priests. But the writer doesn't compare Melchizedek to Aaron. In fact, he says the other priest is "in the order of Melchizedek and not in the order of Aaron" (Hebrews 7:11). The comparison in verse 3 is with the Son of God.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, so I get the pull. But the writer never says Melchizedek is like Moses. He says Melchizedek is "like the Son of God" (Hebrews 7:3). Moses does come up later, when the writer says Moses said nothing about priests from the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:14).

Right on the money, baker. The writer says "Consider how great Melchizedek was," and then points out that "even the patriarch Abraham" gave him a tenth of the plunder (Hebrews 7:4). That word EVEN is doing the heavy lifting. If Abraham, forefather of Israel, hands over a tenth, this is someone worth paying attention to.

The plunder does come up, but the writer never says a word about Abraham's riches here. His point is in the line before: "Consider how great Melchizedek was" (Hebrews 7:4). Giving a tenth to someone shows who's being honored. Abraham's bank account isn't the star of this verse.

explanations.answer: How hard the battle had been
explanations.explanation: It's natural to go there, since the plunder came from a battle. But the writer doesn't say how hard it was. He says "Consider how great Melchizedek was," because even Abraham gave him a tenth (Hebrews 7:4). The spotlight is on Melchizedek, not on the fighting.

You got it, baker. Melchizedek "blessed him who had the promises" (Hebrews 7:6). That's Abraham, and the writer wants us to notice who is doing the blessing. Think about it: the man who holds the promises still receives a blessing from Melchizedek.

Riches is a fair guess, since Abraham had just come back with plunder. But the writer says Melchizedek blessed "him who had the promises" (Hebrews 7:6). The word is promises, not riches. Plunder gets spent, friend, but a promise sticks around.

Armies makes sense with a battle in the background. But that's not the word in the verse. Melchizedek "blessed him who had the promises" (Hebrews 7:6). The writer is pointing at what Abraham was given, not at who marched with him.

Let's flip it, baker. The writer says "the lesser is blessed by the greater" (Hebrews 7:7). Melchizedek is the one handing out the blessing, so he's the greater. The one receiving it is Abraham.

This one is True, baker. The writer says "when Melchizedek met Abraham, Levi was still in the loin of his ancestor" (Hebrews 7:10). Levi wasn't born yet. That's why the writer says, so to speak, that Levi paid the tenth through Abraham (Hebrews 7:9).

You got it, baker! The writer says "on this basis the people received the law" (Hebrews 7:11). So the law and the Levitical priesthood are tied together. That's why verse 12 says that when the priesthood changes, the law must change too.

Land is a good guess, baker, because Israel's story is full of it. But in this verse, the writer says "on this basis the people received the law" (Hebrews 7:11). The law is what's tied to the Levitical priesthood here. The land isn't mentioned.

The temple is a reasonable thing to think of with priests, friend. But the writer doesn't mention a temple in this verse. He says "on this basis the people received the law" (Hebrews 7:11). That's the answer he gives.

Benjamin isn't the tribe the writer names, baker. He says "our Lord descended from Judah" (Hebrews 7:14). Judah is also the tribe that Moses, Israel's leader, said nothing about priests for.
Ephraim isn't the one in the verse, friend. The writer says "our Lord descended from Judah, a tribe as to which Moses said nothing about priests" (Hebrews 7:14). Judah is the answer.

The text says it the other way around, baker. This priest became a priest "not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life" (Hebrews 7:16). He didn't get the job by being in the right family line. His priesthood rests on a life that can't be destroyed.
Good eye, baker. The writer says he became a priest "not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life" (Hebrews 7:16). So it wasn't family line that put him there.

This one is True, friend. The writer says "the former commandment is set aside because it was weak and useless" (Hebrews 7:18). He follows it with "the law made nothing perfect" (Hebrews 7:19). Then he moves straight to the better hope.

Right, baker! "A better hope is introduced, by which we draw near to God" (Hebrews 7:19). That's the good news after the writer says the law made nothing perfect. Drawing near is what the better hope brings.

You've got it, baker. The writer says others became priests without an oath, "but Jesus became a priest with an oath" (Hebrews 7:21). That's what sets His priesthood apart.

explanations.answer: The guarantee of a better covenant
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "Because of this oath, Jesus has become the guarantee of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22). The oath and the guarantee go together. That's a lot of weight resting on what God swore.

explanations.answer: The keeper of the old law
explanations.explanation: The writer goes a different direction, baker. He says the former commandment "is set aside because it was weak and useless" (Hebrews 7:18). Because of the oath, Jesus has become "the guarantee of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22).

Not quite, friend. The writer says Jesus descended from Judah, a tribe Moses said nothing about for priests (Hebrews 7:14). Because of the oath, Jesus has become "the guarantee of a better covenant" (Hebrews 7:22).

Yes, baker. The writer says "because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood" (Hebrews 7:24). The many other priests were replaced because death prevented them from continuing in office (Hebrews 7:23). Jesus lives forever, so His priesthood stays.

explanations.answer: He always lives to intercede for them
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! The writer says Jesus is "able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them" (Hebrews 7:25). The word ALWAYS matters here. He never has to hand the job off.

explanations.answer: He collects a tenth from each of them
explanations.explanation: Collecting a tenth belongs to a different part of the chapter, baker. Melchizedek collected a tenth from Abraham (Hebrews 7:6), and the Levites collected from their brothers (Hebrews 7:5). The reason the writer gives for saving completely is that Jesus "always lives to intercede for them" (Hebrews 7:25).

explanations.answer: He gives them a new law every day
explanations.explanation: That's not in the text, friend. The writer says the law made nothing perfect (Hebrews 7:19). His reason for saving completely is "He always lives to intercede for them" (Hebrews 7:25).

explanations.answer: Once for all by offering up Himself
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "He sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself" (Hebrews 7:27). Notice ONCE FOR ALL. The other high priests had to offer sacrifices daily, first for their own sins and then for the people's.

explanations.answer: Every year on the Day of Atonement
explanations.explanation: A yearly sacrifice isn't what the writer says here, baker. He says the other high priests offered daily sacrifices, but Jesus "sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself" (Hebrews 7:27). Once for all is the answer.

explanations.answer: With the blood of bulls and goats
explanations.explanation: Bulls and goats aren't mentioned in this passage, friend. What the writer says is that Jesus "sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself" (Hebrews 7:27). He gave Himself, one time, for all.
